newsitem.title: USA: Clothing sales boost January results, electronics lag.
newsitem.headline: Clothing sales boost January results, electronics lag.

text.p: Strong clothing sales boosted results at major store chains in January, retailers said Thursday, but as consumers updated their wardrobes, they continued to shun computers and other electronic gear.
Post-holiday clearance sales were minimal since most stores kept inventories in line over Christmas, boding well for fourth quarter profits, industry analysts said.
Weak results in January 1996, when a blizzard pummeled much of the East Coast, helped comparative results.
"I'm impressed," said Howard Eilenberg at Redbook Research, which tracks the retail industry. "I think it was a good month. Of course we expected that."

Salomon Bros.' index of same-store sales, which measures sales at stores open at least a year, rose 7.2 in January, up from a 1.7 percent rise in January 1996. In December, the index showed a 6.1 percent increase.

"On balance, we believe that minimal levels of discounting and strong inventory and expense controls will lead to generally favourable fourth-quarter earnings for the major retailers," Salomon Bros. said in a statement.
The fourth quarter, which includes January at many chains, is when retailers rack up a large chunk of their annual profits.

Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd.'s same sales index rose 6.8 percent at major stores in January but about 3 points came because of easy comparisons with last year by the "Blizzard of the Century" on the East Coast, Mitsubishi said.
Wal-Mart Stores Inc., the nation's largest retailer, said sales for the four weeks ended Jan. 31 rose 14.9 percent to $7.02 billion while same-store sales rose 6.6 percent.

Sears, Roebuck & Co., the second-largest retailer, said same-store sales rose 5.8 percent and that "soft lines," including women's and children's clothing, posted double-digit gains at its larger stores.
Kmart Corp., the No. 3 retailer, said comparable-store sales at its Kmart stores rose 8 percent in January.
Clothing retailers' sales in New York got a boost from a week-long break from the 8.25 percent sales tax on clothing.
Federated Department Stores Inc., which owns the Bloomingdale's and Macy's chains, posted a 9.4 percent same-store increase vs. January 1996.
Analysts said pent-up demand and strong consumer confidence boosted sales of clothing and other items.
"It has been depressed for so long, finally women are saying 'Hey, we have to replace our wardrobes,'" Eilenberg said.
Wisconsin-based department store Kohl's Corp. even got a boost from from the Green Bay Packers' victory in the Super Bowl, reporting that same-store sales jumped 29.5 percent.

"The success of the Green Bay Packers drove many people into our Wisconsin stores looking for Packer merchandise," Chairman William Kellogg said in a statement. "In addition to significant sales in sports apparel, these customers also purchased basic and clearance merchandise."
However, consumer electronics hovered like a black cloud.
Retailers had hoped Intel Corp.'s new multimedia MMX computer chip released in January would give sales a boost, but computers with the new chip were not yet widely available.
"Consumer electronics and home office continue to perform sluggishly in an extremely competitive environment and facing sluggish demand," said Saul Yaari, of Piper Jaffray in Minneapolis.
"MMX has not been a great hit this year, but later on it will," he added, noting computer sales tend to pick up in the second half of the year during the back-to-school season.
Same-store sales at the Best Buy Co. consumer electronics chain fell 15 percent while Circuit City Stores Inc.'s electronics group posted an 11 percent decline.
